A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same micro-macro planar representation and two-stage latent-space training framework, despite the renamed paper and method. All pages, including equations, figures, tables and appendices, are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendices A–B report original novel-view synthesis results, resource measurements, component ablations and stage-specific evaluations on ShapeNet Cars and Basel Faces.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendices B–D report original evaluations across four ShapeNet categories and Basel Faces, including expanded baseline comparisons, CodeNeRF sensitivity results and SPARF failure examples.

M1.justification: Fused-Planes retains v1's micro-macro decomposition, shared base planes, latent/RGB/autoencoder objectives and two-stage optimization. The ULW variant matches v1's macro-only ablation with zero micro features; its promotion and renaming do not establish a new procedure. Algorithm 1 is substantively unchanged.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates ShapeNet Cars and Basel Faces. v2 retains these and adds training/evaluation on ShapeNet Furniture, Speakers and Sofas, substantially broadening represented object categories while retaining the many-view novel-view synthesis task.

E2.justification: The five previous baselines remain. v2 adds 3D Gaussian Splatting, CodeNeRF, the adapted CodeNeRF (MSIG), and SPARF-32/SPARF-128 to reported comparisons. These additions substantially expand the comparison to methods specifically relevant to learning many scenes.

E3.justification: The main NVS comparison changes from 50 sampled scenes per dataset to four per dataset: 16 ShapeNet scenes and four faces. Retained ablations and stage comparisons still use 50. Reported timing changes from four NVIDIA L4 GPUs to a single L4 basis. v2 also introduces CodeNeRF (MSIG)'s 1000-scene initial subset and adds LPIPS to the ablation evaluation; these changes do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The existing component ablations and stage-specific quality checks remain, with the macro-only ablation renamed ULW. v2 adds a limited comparison of 500 versus 1000 initial scenes for CodeNeRF (MSIG) in Appendix C and targeted SPARF texture-failure examples in Appendix D.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seeds, repeated-run counts, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests. Both provide point metrics averaged across sampled scenes. The changed scene sample size and added per-scene tables do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive aggregate and per-scene results for the expanded comparison, including SPARF-128's 0.82-minute training time versus Fused-Planes' 8.96 minutes in Table 1. Changed samples and timing conditions preclude interpreting headline differences as same-setting gains. Stage-specific scores are retained, while the matched ablation table adds LPIPS and changes Tri-Planes SSIM from 0.9512 to 0.953.

T1.justification: The mathematical decomposition, rendering definitions, losses, optimization objectives and common-distribution assumption are retained. Resource formulas are restated using per-scene rates and shared-overhead notation within the same affine scaling model. No new theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation appears.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes the lowest training time and memory footprint against its compared methods. v2 narrows the central claim to resource efficiency among planar representations and competitive costs overall, foregrounding compatibility with image models. It also promotes the existing macro-only setting as ULW with the lowest per-scene memory requirement. This substantially redefines the contribution's scope.

C2.justification: The macro-only setting changes from an ablation illustrating quality degradation to an explicitly useful memory-quality tradeoff. v2 interprets SPARF texture errors through LPIPS and examples, and adds a specific limitation concerning inherited pretrained-VAE biases. v1's explicit suggestion to reduce the initial scene subset as future work is dropped.

D1.justification: v2 identifies Nerfstudio implementations for the single-scene baselines and documents CodeNeRF (MSIG)'s frozen-network, latent-code optimization in Appendix C. The project-page address changes with the method name. Core training hyperparameters remain identical between v1 Tables 7–8 and v2 Tables 13–14.

R1.justification: Section 2 expands substantially into discussions of shared representations and a taxonomy of single-scene, feed-forward and many-scene approaches, supported by a new appendix overview. New positioning against CodeNeRF, SPARF and C3-NeRF accompanies an explicit shared-planar-representation novelty claim. The renamed IG-AE citation refers to the same previously cited work.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten around Fused-Planes and multi-scene inverse graphics. Related work is reorganized into multiple subsections, the experimental narrative is rebuilt around baseline categories, and appendix organization expands. These changes substantially alter the narrative beyond terminology replacement.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main layout, redraws Figure 1 around per-scene costs with planar/non-planar distinctions, and restructures the main comparison table. It expands scaling plots and qualitative comparisons, adds per-scene tables and image grids, and introduces texture-failure close-ups. The architecture diagram is largely retained with revised labels and caption.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence and positioning behind the central efficiency contribution. Adding SPARF and CodeNeRF exposes important competing resource advantages and supports narrowing v1's broad lowest-cost message to planar representations. Additional object categories, per-scene results and failure examples improve scrutiny. The reduction from 50 to four scenes per dataset in the main comparison, without uncertainty estimates, limits generalization; nevertheless, the expanded relevant comparisons and better-calibrated contribution resolve an important weakness of v1.
